questions.prompt: Why does the book treat alignment and connection as a separate superpower?
choices: Because one committed team is not enough when several teams must move together
Because commitment no longer matters once teamwork begins
Because every team should own the same objective

explanation.gentle: The chapter begins when one-team force has to become cross-team coordination.
explanation.direct: Alignment matters because several teams can still interfere with one another after commitment.
explanation.competitive: One strong team inside a disconnected system is still not enough.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter define alignment?
choices: Identical goals for every team
Visible shared direction connecting related team priorities
Silence about dependencies until they appear

explanation.gentle: The chapter says alignment connects priorities across teams.
explanation.direct: It is related work under visible shared direction, not sameness.

questions.prompt: Why is forced sameness a weak substitute for alignment?
choices: Because the chapter says teams should stay completely independent
Because alignment connects differentiated work without flattening local expertise
Because visibility makes every team identical anyway

explanation.gentle: Different teams can still move together without doing identical work.
explanation.direct: The chapter protects specialization while insisting on visible connection.
explanation.competitive: Sameness is neat-looking but weaker than real coordination.

questions.prompt: Quinn sees three teams with separate plans and unclear handoffs. What best fits the chapter?
choices: The teams are aligned because each one has serious goals
The teams need visible connected priorities before calling the effort coordinated
The teams should hide their dependencies to avoid conflict

explanation.gentle: Serious local plans are weaker than shared visible connection.
explanation.direct: The missing piece is cross-team visibility, not more separate effort.

questions.prompt: A robotics council worked hard in separate lanes and discovered conflicts late. What chapter failure does this show?
choices: Healthy specialization with no downside
Disconnected priorities and hidden dependencies
Too much visible shared direction

explanation.gentle: The problem is not low effort but weak connection.
explanation.direct: The council lacked visible links between subgroup objectives.

questions.prompt: Which misreading does the chapter reject?
choices: Alignment is bureaucratic sameness
Alignment requires visible connected priorities
Alignment exposes dependencies early

explanation.gentle: The chapter separates alignment from flattening every team into the same work.
explanation.direct: Bureaucratic sameness is a weaker substitute than real connection.
explanation.competitive: If sameness is your definition, you missed the mechanism.

questions.prompt: What is happening when teams work hard but cannot see how their objectives affect one another?
choices: Real teamwork is already complete
Siloed sincerity is creating preventable friction
The chapter says visibility no longer matters

explanation.gentle: Hidden links let sincere teams still weaken one another.
explanation.direct: The chapter treats private priorities and unclear dependencies as the key problem.
explanation.competitive: Good motives still crash when the map stays private.

questions.prompt: A volunteer network wants shared direction without forcing identical plans on every team. Which judgment best fits the chapter?
choices: The network should avoid cross-team visibility
The network should connect differentiated work under visible shared direction
The network should require every team to own the same goals

explanation.gentle: Alignment can connect different work without erasing it.
explanation.direct: The chapter favors visible links over identical tasks.

questions.prompt: What deeper point does the chapter make about dependency visibility?
choices: It belongs only to project management and not to OKRs
It helps teams catch tradeoffs, duplicate effort, and conflict before collision
It matters only after teams have already collided

explanation.gentle: The chapter makes visibility part of how teamwork gets stronger.
explanation.direct: Dependency visibility matters because it changes coordination before the cost rises.
explanation.competitive: See the ambush early or pay for it later.

questions.prompt: Why does Chapter 7 naturally lead into the MyFitnessPal story next?
choices: Because the theory of alignment now needs a company case
Because alignment no longer needs examples
Because teamwork ends with this superpower chapter

explanation.gentle: The next chapter turns the superpower into a concrete company case.
explanation.direct: After the concept is clear, the book tests it inside MyFitnessPal.
explanation.competitive: Now the case has to earn the theory.
